full_judgment:
The respondent No.1 to 3 who are partners of the registered firm named and styled as M/s. Masood Reza and Co. (hereinafter referred to as "the firm") filed an application under Article 102 of the Constitution for directing the appellant and respondents No.4 to 8 to restore to them the possession, control and management of this firm in pursuance of an order of release of the same by the Government (as contained in NOTIFICATION No. SRO. 31-L/76 No. Industries/13-3M/104/75/11 dated 17-1-76 together with all papers, documents and properties both moveable and immovable. The said firm used to carry on export, import, indenting and commission agency business. 

 Ministry of Industries Nationalised Industries Division Dacca, the 27th January, 1975. No. S.R.O. 60-L/75/F/ST-E. 8/72. In exercise of the powers conferred by clause (1) of Article 10 of the Bangladesh Industrial Enterprises (Nationalisation) Order, 1972 (President's Order No.27 of 1972) the Government is pleased to place M/s. Mohammad Masood Reza & Co. Dacca under the Bangladesh Steel Mills Corporation. 

 GOVERNMENT OF THE PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF BANGLADESH Cabinet Secretariat, Cabin Division NOTIFICATION. 

 S.R.O.70-L/76/F/ST-1.8/72, in exercise of the powers conferred by Article 10(1) (d) of Bangladesh Industrial Enterprises (Nationalisation) Order, 1972 (President's Order No.27 of 1972), read with section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 (X of 1897), the Government is pleased to cancel the Ministry of Industries, Nationalised Industries Division's NOTIFICATION No.S.R.O.60-L/75/ST/1.8/72 dated January 27, 19, 75. 

 5. This NOTIFICATION, as quoted above, shows that it was issued in exercise of the powers conferred by Article 10(1) (d) of the Industrial Enterprises (Nationalisation) Order, 1972, P. O. No.27 of 1972 read with section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897. After the firm was so released by the Government the respondents No.1 to 3 requested the Ministry of Industries (Nationalised Industries Division) and also the appellant to deliver possession of the firm to them. 

 Ref: Ministry of Industries, Government of Bangladesh NOTIFICATION No.Shilpa/13-3M/104/75/11 Dated 17-1-1976. 

 7. On behalf of the respondent No.4, it was stated that after the order of release they received a representation from the appellant that if the firm of the respondents No.1 to 3 is released they would face difficulties in running the industrial unit of M/s. Md. Masood Reza Group of Industries. Further, the entire master was being examined by the Government and they have no mala fide intention to frustrate or defeat the legitimate claim of the respondents No.1 to 3. 

 9. The rule nisi came up for hearing before a Bench of the High Court Division which by an order dated 6th May, 1977 made the Rule absolute and directed the delivery of physical possession of the firm to the respondents No.1 to 3 and also made absolute the interim order of injunction restraining the appellant and the respondents No.4 to 8 from dealing with the firm. It was found by the High Court that the appellant which was a statutory corporation was bound, by the order of release made by the Government arid that the difficulties which were alleged by the appellant could be resolved by mutual discussions. It was observed that "as no case has been made out that there is any lien of anybody in the firm the financial involvement can be sorted out either mutually or by way of civil proceeding but that would not stand in the way of issuing the writ as has been prayed for". 

 3. Whether the appellant has any locus standi to dispute the validity of the orders made or the directions given by the Government of Bangladesh. 

 11. Mr. S.R. Pal, Counsel for the appellant, submitted that once the property in question vested in the Government according to the provisions of the Abandoned Property Order, 1972, it had no jurisdiction to release the same, there being no provisions enabling the Government to do so. For the release of this firm, the respondents No.1 to 3 could only avail of the remedy as provided in the aforesaid Order. The learned Counsel next contended that apart from the absence of any provisions enabling the release of property, there was further difficulty in the way of the Government releasing such property once it has been placed with any corporation under article 10(1) (d) of the Nationalisation Order, 1972. Thus, according to him, there are two bars in the way of the Government to release any property placed under the control of any Statutory Corporation under the provisions of the Nationalisation Order, whether abandoned or not. 

 12. The learned Counsel also contended that, the Government had no power either under the Nationalisation Order or section 21 of the General Clauses Act to cancel the order of placement of any property under the provisions of article 10(1) (d) and (1A) of the Nationalisation Order; nor, having regard to the provisions of (1A) of article 10 of the Nationalisation Order, can the respondents No.1 to 3 challenge the vesting of the property in the Government. 

 13. Mr. S.R. Pal, finally contended that the appellant which is not department of Government but a statutory corporation is not bound by any order of the Government which is in excess of the powers given under the Nationalisation Order or any other statute. Its entity being separate and distinct from that of the Government, it can raise the question of the validity of the order of release as well as of cancellation of placement dated 11-2-76. Since the order of release and cancellation directly affect the appellant, it has the locus standi to challenge the same. As the appellant invested its own fund in the affairs of the firm in question it had direct interest in the matter. It was further pointed out by the Counsel that since the appellant was made a party to the petition under Article 102 of the Constitution the appellant had locus standi to question the validity of the impugned orders. 

 14. In support of his contentions mentioned above, the learned counsel referred to the relevant NOTIFICATIONs issued by the Government since the respondent’s firm was taken over by it on 7th March, 1972. These NOTIFICATIONs have already been mentioned and quoted above. The two main NOTIFICATIONs with which Mr. Pal were concerned are the, NOTIFICATIONs dated 17th January, 1976 which released the film in favour of the respondents No.1 to 3 and the NOTIFICATION dated 11th February, 1976 which cancelled the earlier NOTIFICATION dated 27th January, 1975 by which the firm was placed under the Steel Mills Corporation. As regards the contention that the Government has no power to release any property vested in the Government as abandoned property, the learned Counsel referred to the decision reported in 27 DLR 468. He went so far as to suggest that even if any property which could not be taken over by the Government as an abandoned property as defined it the Abandoned Property Order, 1972, but has been treated as such, it cannot be released by the Government of its own motion. It is true that having regard to the provisions of the Abandoned Property Order, which provided or vesting of the abandoned property in the Government and also set the machinery for releasing the same, no proper which falls within the definition of abandoned property as given in article 2(1) of the said Order can be released by the Government excepting in accordance with the procedure laid down in the said Order or under any other statute which may enable the Government to do so. Simple as this proposition is which is not also disputed by any one, the real question is whether this can lead to the inference that the Government must be denied the power of release any property forthwith, if it appears that any property taken over as an abandoned property was not in fact an abandoned property at the time it was taken over as such. Or, in other words, whether there is any difference between a property which is an abandoned property within the meaning of the same expression used in article 2(1) of the Abandoned Property Order and any property which is merely treated as abandoned property. Mr. Pal submitted that once any property is taken over as abandoned property it becomes an abandoned property and vests absolutely in the Government, as provided in Article 4 of the Abandoned Property Order which says "on the commencement of this Order all abandoned properties in Bangladesh shall vest in the Government and shall be administered, controlled, managed and disposed of, by transfer or otherwise, in accordance with the provision of this Order." The question is whether the expressions "all abandoned properties used in this article mean such properties as come within the definition of abandoned properties in article 2(1) of the same Order or any property which though not covered by this definition, is treated as abandoned property. Article 2(1) provides as follows: 

 (a) any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh; 

 (b) any property which is in the possession or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force. Explanation: "Person who is not present in Bangladesh" includes anybody of persons or Company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's REPUBLIC OF BANGLADESH." 

 15. On a proper consideration of these provisions, it would appear that unless any property answers the description of abandoned property, the merely taking of such property on the assumption or mistaken belief that it falls within that description will not vest it in the Government, the obvious reason being that, in the case of such property no occasion arises for the application of the Abandoned Property Order. As was pointed out by the learned Counsel for the respondents No.1 to 3 that if on a wrong assumption or by mistake any property has been taken over as abandoned property, it is not required to take recourse to the remedy provided in the Order itself. A mere representation by the owner of such property should suffice to get the property released. 

 16. Mr. Pal submitted that in view of the provisions of Article 15(1) of the Abandoned Property Order the owner of any property which is treated by the Government as abandoned property must apply to the Government for its release as provided in that article. Article 15(1) provides as follows: 

 "15. (1) Any person claiming any right or interest in any property treated by Government as abandonee property may make an application to the prescribed authority on the ground that- 

 17. If these provisions are duly considered, it would appear that they do not take away the power of the Government to release any property suo motu if it appears that any property which it had taken over was not in fact an abandoned cannot be intended to have enabled the Government to retain any property which does not fall within the definition of abandoned property in the Abandoned Property Order merely because the Government had somehow or other taken it over as such and the aggrieved owner had somehow failed to follow the aforesaid procedure. It is not, however, true that the respondents No.1 to 3 did not make any representation to the Government for release of their firm after it had been taken over by the Government. A number of letters which have been annexed to the petition, under Article 102, Annexure 1 to IX, show that the respondents No.1 to 3 were moving the Government for release of their firm. An enquiry by the Government was also held in the middle of May, 1973. 

 18. As regards the contention that the property in question was validly taken over by the Government as abandoned property it is necessary to mention the NOTIFICATION dated, 7th March, 1972 quoted earlier, which mentions that "in partial modification of the NOTIFICATION No.1A (80)72-282 dated 18th February, 1972 of this Ministry and in exercise of the authority given by the Acting President's Order No. Sec.-XI/IM-35/71/17 dated 30th December, 1971 the Ministry of Industries is pleased to take over with immediate effect and until further orders the management of M/s. E. Pak Traders, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dacca M/s. Masood Reza & Co. Reza Chamber, 75, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dacca." 

 GOVERNMENT OF THE PEOPLE'S 

 GOVERNMENT OF THE PEOPLE'S 

 Since it is not necessary to hold whether, the Acting President Order No.1 was impliedly repealed by the Abandoned Property Order 1972, it would be sufficient to say that the preservation and protection of the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 by the Constitution were considered necessary to protect any action taken under that order and not for continuing its operation after the Abandoned Property Order 1972, came into force. Moreover, the Abandoned Property Order provided all necessary legislative authorisation for taking over all properties which were abandoned or had already been taken over under the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1973. It, therefore, follows that on March 7, 1972, the date of taking over of the respondent’s firm Government would not take it over as abandoned property purporting to exercise its powers under the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972. It appears that the respondent's firm which was not taken over under the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 before the commencement of the Abandoned Property Order, could no longer be looked upon as abandoned property. 

 23. From the expressions "any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972)" used in Article 2(1)(ii) of the Abandoned Property Order, it would seem that they refer to past action and not any action in the future. It would, therefore, appear that they mean any property which had already been taken over under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 and would not mean any property which shall be taken over under that Order in future after the Abandoned Property Order came into force. On and from 26th February, 1972 when the Abandoned Property Order of 1972 (P.O. 16/72) was promulgated, any property which was owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property will be abandoned property. Such property will also include (i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a state which was at war with Bangladesh and (ii) any property taken-over under the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972. Any property which answered the above mentioned definition of abandoned property in the Abandoned Property Order was to vest in the Government on the commencement of this Order. In these circumstances, the order of release by the Government of the respondent's firm cannot be held to be void and illegal. 

 24. The next contention of Mr. Pal. Counsel for the appellant, was that once the Government has placed any property, taken over as abandoned property under the appellant, which is one of the Corporations set up under Article 10(1) (d) of the Nationalisation Order, 1972, the Government has no power to cancel the order of placement as by such placement the property becomes vested in the Government. Article 10(a) (d) of the Nationalisation Order is as follows: 

 (4) Bangladesh Steel Mills Corporations; which shall respectively have and exercise the powers of a Corporation in respect of such industrial enterprises, including industrial enterprises owned wholly or partly by the Government or vested in Government under the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 or owned and managed by a statutory corporation, which the Government may place under it by an order notified in the official Gazette." 

 (i) are owned wholly or partly by the Government, or 

 (ii) vested in the Government under the Abandoned Property Order, 1972, or 

 26. Mr. Pal, submitted that among the three categories of industrial enterprises which can be placed by the Government under the appellant corporation, the respondents firm falls under the second category. It has already been seen that the respondent's firm did not lawfully vest in the Government under the Abandoned Property Order 1972. It was neither wholly nor partly owned by Government, nor was it owned and managed by a statutory corporation before it was placed under the appellant. Having been outside any of these categories as the above, how the respondent's firm, it has been rightly asked, could at all be placed by the Government under the aforesaid article. Being confronted with this difficulty Mr. Pal next submitted that as soon as any industrial enterprises is placed under a corporation by an order under clause 1 of Article 10 of the Nationalisation Order, it vests in the Government which then, has no power to divest it irrespective of whether it had lawfully vested in the Government as an abandoned property under the provisions of the Abandoned Property Order, 1972. He first referred to the unamended provisions of Article 4 of the Nationalisation Order, 1972, which runs as follows: 

 "On the commencement of this order, all the shares in each of the scheduled industrial enterprises or, as the case may be, the industrial enterprises placed under a corporation by an Order under clause (1) of Article 10, which have not already vested in the Government by or under any other law for the time being, in force, shall, by virtue of this Article and without further assurance, stand vested in and allotted to the Government free of any trust, mortgage, charge, lien, interest to other encumbrance whatsoever and the government free from such commencement, be the sole shareholder of such industrial enterprises." 

 "4. (1) All such share and other proprietary interests in each of the scheduled industrial enterprise, and all such industrial enterprises paced under a Corporation by or by an order under clause (1) of article 10, and all shares and proprietary and other interests, as have not already vested in the Government by or under any law for the time being in force, shall by virtue of this Article and without any further proceeding or formality, stand vested in, and allotted to, the Government free of any trust, mortgage, charge, lien, interest or other encumbrance whatsoever,— 

 b) in the case of an industrial enterprise placed under a Corporation by order under clause (1) of Article 10, on the date on which it is so placed; and subject to the provisions of clause (2), the Government shall, as from such commencement or date, be the sole shareholder in or owner of, such industrial enterprises. 

 (2) The Government may, if in the national interest it deems it expedient, so to do, sell or otherwise transfer to any person, on such terms and conditions as may be settled with him. any industrial enterprise or any share or proprietary or other interest in such an enterprise, vested in the Government under clause (1): 

 (3) Where the Government sells or otherwise transfers under clause (2) wholly or partly, any industrial enterprises, or any share or proprietor or other interest in an industrial enterprise, it may by NOTIFICATION in the official Gazette, omit from the schedule, or, as the case may be, withdraw from the Corporation under which it was placed by an order under clause (1) of Article 10, that industrial enterprise. 

 (4) Where a NOTIFICATION under clause (3) is issued in respect of any industrial enterprise, the Government may;— 

 (a) by the same NOTIFICATION or by a separate NOTIFICATION direct that the provisions of articles 5, 6, 7 and 8 shall cease to apply or shall apply with such NOTIFICATION or qualification as may be specified in the NOTIFICATION, to such industrial enterprise and (b) take such measures, including consequential changes in the relevant memorandum or articles of association, as may be necessary to restore, as far as the changed circumstances may permit, to the legal position of the industrial enterprise under the Companies Act, 1913 (VII of 1913) as obtained before it vested in the Government under clause(1)". 

 28. From clause 1 of the aforesaid provisions, the learned Counsel wanted to show that even if the respondents firm had not already vested in the Government by or under any law for the time being in force, i.e. Abandoned Property Order, 1972, it stood vested in the Government as soon as it was placed under the appellant corporation. Secondly, clause 2 of the aforesaid provisions only permitted the Government to sell or otherwise transfer each industrial enterprise as is placed under a corporation under article 10(1) of the Nationalisation Order in the manner laid down there-in. Since the Government did not take recourse to this clause in the present case, its clients not in accordance with law and as such invalid. 

 29. Since in our opinion the very basis for treating the respondent’s firm as abandoned property was lacking and since also there was no basis for placing it under a corporation, the aforesaid provisions can have no manner of application in relation to impugned actions of the Government. This observation applies with equal force to the proviso which was added to clause (1A) of article 10 by Ordinance No.1 of 1976, which is quoted further below in this judgment. 

 30. It is difficult to understand how if any industrial enterprise does not fall within any of the three categories mentioned in Article 10(1) (d) of the Nationalisation Order, 1973 as mentioned above, such industrial enterprise would vest in the Government simple because it has been placed under any statutory corporation set up under the provisions of Article 10 of that Order. Unless the conditions laid down therein or elsewhere in the Order are fulfilled, the mere placing of an industrial enterprise under a corporation set up by the Government for managing nationalised industrial enterprises cannot be said to have vested it in the Government. The provisions, of the Nationalisation Order No.1972 can have no manner of application to an enterprise which is not an industrial enterprise falling in one or the other category. 

 31. Referring to the preamble of the Nationalisation Order, 1972. Mr. Pal submitted that Government has power to place any new industrial enterprise under any of the Corporations set up under Article 10(1) (d) of the same Order. The preamble to the Nationalisation Order No.1972 provides: 

 32. Since the entire contention so long has been based on the denial of the Government's power to cancel the order of placement because the firm of the respondent No.1 to 3 vested in the Government as an abandoned property, it is too late in the day to say that the 'Government has also the power to place any new industrial enterprise under the statutory corporation established under the Nationalisation Order. The respondent’s firm does neither come under the expressions "some other enterprises" nor under the expressions "New industrial enterprises" used in the preamble to the Nationalisation Order. Moreover, the preamble cannot control the operative provisions of Article 10(1) (d) which have clearly enumerated three categories of enterprises which can be placed by the Government under any of the corporations set up under that article. 

 33. Mr. Pal also referred to the provisions of clause (1A) of Article 10 of the Nationalisation Order and submitted that once any industrial enterprise has been placed under any corporation under article 10(1)(d) it shall be deemed to have vested in the Government and the Order of placement cannot be challenged in any court of law. The provisions of clause (1A) areas follow: 

 "(A) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, an industrial enterprise, placed under any corporation by an order notified in the official Gazette under sub-clause (d) of clause (1) of Article 10, and all charges or other proprietary interest in such industrial enterprise shall be deemed to have always vested in the Government and such order shall be challenged on the ground that the industrial enterprise or the shares or interest therein had not vested in the Government, or that the industrial enterprise, or any share or interest therein was not liable to be vested in the Government: 

 Provided that the Government may, at anytime transfer an industrial enterprise mentioned in this clause and all shares or other proprietory interest therein, in such manner and on such condition as it may deem fit, to the person who owned such industrial enterprise and shares or interest before they were vested in the Government, if such persons are Bangalees and the industrial enterprise and the shares or interest therein were vested in the Government under the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal Order), 1972 (P.O.No. 16 of 1972) prior to the placement of the industrial enterprise under any Corporation, and on such transfer the industrial enterprise shall cane to be under the control of any Corporation." 

 34. From the expressions "shall be deemed to have always vested In the Government" Mr. Pal wanted to assert that event if the respondents firm be found not to have vested in the Government under provisions of the Abandoned Property Order, once the firm has been placed under Article 10(1)(d) of the Nationalisation Order, 1972, it shall be deemed to have vested in the Government and such vesting cannot be challenged on the ground that it did not vest nor was it liable to be vested in the Government. Had the appellant's claim that the respondent's firm had vested in the Government as an abandoned property been found in fact, there might have been some substance in the contention of the learned Counsel. Since the appellant's claim has been found to be untenable, the mere placement of the respondents firm under the Corporation under Article 10(1) (d) does not invest it with the qualities or status of any of the categories mentioned therein and, therefore, consequently does not empower the Government to retain it. Such claim to retain, if conceded, would amount to putting premium on the illegal seizure of the citizen's property. It requires to be known to all concerned that the property of a citizen can neither be acquired nor be retained by the Government unless it is done under proper legislative authorisation. The seizure of property without legislative sanction whether by a private citizen or the Government amounts to illegal grabbing. A citizen's property cannot be seized also under the colourable exercise of power conferred by the legislature. 

 35. Apart from the absence of any legal basis for placing the respondent’s firm under Article 10(1) (d) as, in fact it is not an abandoned property, it appears that so far as placement of such property is concerned, it is illegal also on the ground that in so far as the respondents, firm is not an industrial enterprise the Government lacks the necessary power to place it under Article 10(1)(d) of the Nationalisation Order, 1972, for, this Article empowers the Government to place only such industrial enterprise as are mentioned therein. Under this article Government has no power to place any enterprise under a statutory corporation which is a commercial firm. In their petition under Article 102 of the Constitution the respondents have all through claimed that their firm is a commercial concern. Moreover, Mr. T.K. Khan, Counsel for the respondents, referred to the following NOTIFICATION wherein it has been admitted by the Government that on scrutiny the respondent’s firm was found to be a commercial unit which should, therefore, be handed over to the Ministry of Commerce. 

 "GOVERNMENT OF THE PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF BANGLADESH 

 The Ministry of Trade & Commerce (Commerce Division) GOVERNMENT OF THE PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF BANGLADESH, Dacca. 

 36. A copy of this letter was also sent to the appellant. The aforesaid NOTIFICATION supports the respondents claim that their firm is a Commercial firm, and not an industrial enterprise. It, therefore, appear that such firm cannot be placed under any of the corporations set up by the Government under Article 10 (1) (d) as mentioned above. 

 37. Subsequently also from correspondences between the Ministry of Industry and the Ministry of Commerce it appears that the commercial nature of the respondent’s concern was admitted by the Government. On January 10, 1975 the Ministry of Industries wrote the following letter requesting the Ministry of Commerce to hand over possession of the respondent’s firm to the appellant as it was placed under the latter: 

 GOVERNMENT OF THE PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF BANGLADESH 

 GOVERNMENT OF THE PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF BANGLADESH 

 39. As regards the power of the Government to cancel the order of placement under Artie e 10(1) (d) of the Nationalisation Order, Mr. Pal, submitted that since such placement created rights in favour of the appellant, the Government cannot withdraw or rescind it without the appellant's consent. In support, he cited the case of Pakistan Vs. Md. Niayamat-ullah Faruki, (1969) 21 DLR, SC 238. This decision, relied upon in a recent case reported in (1975) 28 DLR 350 by the High Court, concerns the vesting of rights in a Government servant. Such rights which vested in him under order of the appropriate Ministry of the Government was sought to be nullified by an order the Ministry of Finance on the ground that they were not consulted before conferring such rights. On the latter's objection the order originally passed by the appropriate Ministry fixing the initial pay of the Government servant concerned was withdrawn. This decision is not, therefore, applicable to the facts of the present case. 

 40. Here, no right is created in favour of the appellant corporation to retain the respondent’s firm. The Government can place a property of any of the descriptions mentioned in Article 10(1) (d) of the Nationalisation Order, 1972 under a corporation and it can as well withdraw the same from it. Such withdrawal does not require the consent of corporation, whether prior or subsequent. Such property after placement, vests in the Government, not in any corporation and also, after withdrawal it remains vested in the Government, excepting, of course, in any case like the present. Since we already exhaustively dealt with the extent of the Government's power to release the same we need not further consider that question. 

 41. As regards the third contention as to the locus standi of the appellant to dispute the validity of the orders of cancellation and release, Mr. Pal, Counsel for the appellant, vehemently argued that since the appellant is a statutory corporation, it is a separate and distinct entity and can, therefore, challenge the Government's power and competence to pass the impugned orders. In order to substantiate the appellants claim that being a statutory corporation it is not bound to obey any order passed by the Government, particularly of the nature of orders passed by it, Mr. Pal, referred to almost all the provisions of Nationalisation Order, 1972, beginning from its preamble. He particularly mentioned articles 7, 10, 11, 12, 17, 20, 11, 22 and 25 of the same Order. 

 In this connection he also referred to English decisions, namely Robertson Vs. Minister of Pensions, (1948) 2 All. E. R. 76M (1949) 1KB 227 and Howell Vs. Falmouth Boat Construction Ltd. (1951) 2 All E.R. 278 and submitted that the former decision which laid down the principle that one department of the Government was bound by the order parsed by another department of the Government, both being agents of the Crown was overruled by the later decision from which he quoted the following passage from Lord Simon's Judgment: 

 "The illegality of an act is the same whether or not the sector has been misled by an assumption of authority on the part of a Government Officer however high or low in the hierarchy. 1 do not doubt that in criminal proceedings it would be a material factor that the actor had been thus misled if knowledge was a necessary element of the offence and in any case it would have a bearing the sentence to be imposed, but that is not the question. The question is whether the character of an act done in face of a statutory prohibition is affected by the fact that it has been induced by a misleading assumption of authority. In my opinion, the answer is clearly: No. Such an answer may make more difficult the task of the citizen who is anxious to walk in the narrow way, but that does not justify a different answer being given. I am, therefore, of opinion that the order of the Court of Appeal cannot be sustained for the reasons given by Denning, LJ. 

 44. Without entering into any dispute as to whether the case of Robertson Vs. Minister of Pensions was overruled by House of Lords in the Howell's case, it seems to us that the principle stated therein has not been assailed before us. In the present case the problem is not Whether one department of the Government should be estopped from challenging any order passed by another department of the Government on me ground that me former passed an illegal order, rather the issue is whether a statutory corporation which is subject to the superintendence and control by the Government can dispute the validity of an order passed by the Government. Or, in other words, what is the nature of relationship between the Government and the Statutory Corporation with regard to a matter about which the Corporation has no concern. As already seen the power to place any industrial enterprise under any of the Corporation set up under article 10(1) (d) of the Nationalisation order or withdraw it belonged exclusively to the Government. Such power was not shared by the Corporation which has, therefore, no option or choice in respect of such placement. Its duty as laid down by the several provisions of the Nationalisation Order is merely to administer an industrial enterprise placed under it by the Government. If the Government withdraws any industrial enterprise from any corporation it is none of the concern of the corporation to challenge it nor to claim that as soon as it was placed under it such enterprise vested in it. From the provisions quoted above, it is clear that as soon as an industrial enterprise is placed under any corporation it either vests or shall be deemed to have vested in the Government. If, therefore, the Government has cancelled the order of placement, of the respondents firm under the appellant, if has no cause for grievance nor should it be grieved, if after such cancellation the Government deals with the enterprise so withdrawn in any way it likes. 

 45. Though the appellant was in the position of respondent in the petition under Article 102 of the Constitution and as such has claimed, the power to resist the impugned Orders, its stand is not justified for the simple reason that it could not be said to be an "aggrieved party" within the meaning of the expressions used in Article 102 of the constitution. If instead of the respondent’s challenge finder Article 102 the appellant chose to challenge the impugned orders by filing a Writ petition, it could not be held to aggrieved by the Government action. And for the same reason the appellant though was made a respondent in the petition under Article 102 of the Constitution, cannot be allowed to challenge the legality or validity of the impugned orders particularly when such petition was filed against its refusal to comply with the aforesaid orders. A statutory corporation enjoys such autonomy as has been granted by the statute and can exercise authority within the ambit of the power given to it by the statute. The matter of placing an industrial enterprise and subsequent withdrawal of such an enterprise from is not within the jurisdiction of the statutory corporation set up under Articles 10(1) (d). It can exercise so much authority in relation to such an enterprise as has been conferred on it and that also as long as it has not been withdrawn from it after its placement. The principle of autonomy which a corporation enjoys under the statute creating it cannot be claimed to militate against the exercise of power by the Government in respect of matters covered by the principle. 

 46. Mr. Pal, Counsel for the appellant, referred to 'text book on’ ''Administrative Law" by H. W.R. Wade, 3rd Edition, PP. 43-44 (1971) wherein legal independence of statutory corporations has been considered. As no question involving the exercise of the power of internal management of the appellant corporation is involved in the present case, it is not necessary for us to find its degree of independence vis-a-vis the Government. How wide or precarious is the legal independence of statutory corporation like the appellants need not be defined in view of a matter which is external to the corporation's jurisdiction. 

 47. A Statutory Corporation cannot claim any power to call in question the Government's power to place an industrial enterprise under the control and supervision or its withdrawal after such placement. 

 Mr. K. A. Bakr, the learned Attorney-General, appeared on behalf of the Government but instead of supporting the impugned orders passed by the Government, advanced reasons in support of the appellant. He did this under Government instructions. Mention may be made that the appeal by the Government was filed after the Attorney-General was served with a notice to appear when the leave petition by the Chairman of the Steel Mills Corporation was being heard. In order to explain why the Government did not make any submissions before the learned Judges of the High Court excepting filing an affidavit in opposition the learned Attorney General submitted that as the prayer for adjournment of delivery of the judgment of the High Court was not conceded to by the learned Judges, the Deputy Attorney-General who appeared for the Government, could not place the relevant files of the Government to explain the necessity for holding up the delivery of the possession of the respondent’s firm. He further submitted that as the firm was placed by the Government under the corporation according to the provisions of the Nationalisation Order, 1972 all interest of the respondents 1 to 3 in the firm vested in the Government under Article 10(1) (d) read with Article 4 of the aforesaid order. The impugned order of release under Article 15(2) of the Abandoned Property Order was, therefore, wrongly made. His submission is that the Government admitted that it gave the order of release not according to law and that the objections raised by the Corporation were correct. He referred to a statement made in the notice demanding justice served by the respondents on the Government as well as the other appellant which says that the respondent’s firm vested in the Government after it was placed under the corporation under Article 10(1) (d) of the Nationalisation Order. His submission which proceeded on the same line as Mr. Pal's were however, brief and related to the legality of the impugned orders of release and cancellation of the placement of the respondent’s firm under the corporation. Since we have already dealt with these questions, there is no further necessity to consider them over again. Before parting with the case it may, however, be mentioned that the present case offered a hard choice to the Court inasmuch as the Government's order was at the first instance not implemented by a statutory corporation which was bound to implement it and secondly, that the Government itself did not come forward in support of the order made by itself. Between the date on which the order was made and the date of filing the Writ petition there was a sufficient gap. Nothing was done by the Government in rescinding the same during this period. Even the Government did not file an appeal in time which was only filed after notice was served by the Court upon the Attorney General during the hearing of the leave petition. There is no precedence, as was admitted by the learned Attorney-General, of opposition by a Statutory Corporation to a Government order particularly when it is passed by the Secretary to the Ministry. 

 Debesh Chandra Bhattacharya J.—I have perused the judgment prepared by my learned brother Mr. Justice Munim and concur with him in the final order prepared by him for the dismissal of the appeal, but I regret to say with respect that I have been unable to agree with the answer given by him in respect of the last of the three questions, for which special leave was granted, namely, the locus-standi of the Corporation to dispute the validity of the impugned orders made by the Government. As regards the two other questions, I agree with the conclusions reached by him, but I think, I should very briefly, give for such conclusions, my own reasons, which are a bit different in certain respects from those of my learned brother. I have not recounted the facts of the case, as they have been set out with proper details in the judgment of my learned brother. 

 50. On this question Mr. Pal learned Counsel for the Corporation has contended firstly, that having regard to the provisions of article 15 of the President's Order No.16 of 1972 and the rules framed thereunder there was no proceeding under the said article which was to be initiated within three months of the date of the commencement of the Order before the prescribed authority, i. e the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub Divisional Officer within whose Jurisdiction the property was situated and as such there could be no valid order under article 15 of the said Order and secondly that in any event the properties in question having been vested in the Government by virtue of provisions of President's Order No.16 of 1972 the Government was not competent in any view of the matter to make the impugned order of release, which purports to divest the Government of such properties. 

 52. A proceeding under article 15 presupposes the taking over of a certain property as abandoned property. On the promulgation of President's Order No.16 of 1972, all properties which were abandoned properties within the meaning of article 2 of the Order vested in the Government of Bangladesh. The Government has no right to release the property which has vested in it as an abandoned property but the prescribed authority under article 15 can release the property only when it comes to a finding that the property to be released, though treated as an abandoned property, was not really an abandoned property and as such it did not vest in the Government. The impugned order does not show that it was the result of Such a finding nor does it appear to have been made by the prescribed authority in a proper proceeding under article 15. In the circumstances, the contention of the learned Counsel that the impugned order cannot be treated to be valid order under article 15 seems to be a force. 

 53. But this answer does not finally dispose of the question, as the question still remaining to be answered is whether the order of release can be said to be otherwise lawful, if the properties released were not really abandoned properties. Learned Counsel for the Corporation has submitted that article 15 read with article 16 is the only remedial provision for release of a property taken over as an abandoned property, no matter whether it was really an abandoned property or not and that there having been no such proceeding as contemplated in article 15 the Government has no jurisdiction to release such a property. 

 54. I am not prepared to accept such an extremely mechanical proposition which looks merely for the form, rather than the substance of a matter. A property taken over as an abandoned property will not ipso facto vest in the Government. Under article 4 of President's Order No.15 of 1972 all abandoned properties within the meaning of article 2(1) of the Order vested in the Government of Bangladesh on the commencement of the Order. If any property, which has been taken over and treated as an abandoned property is not in fact an abandoned property within the meaning of the Order, it has certainly not vested in the Government. The Government has not acquired any right or authority in respect of such a property. In such a circumstance, the Government must be deemed to be not in lawful occupation of such a property and shall be, under the general law, accountable to the rightful owner for depriving him of the profits and gains of the property, subject to the provisions of article 23 of the Order which gives legislative protection to the Government and any person for anything done in good faith under the Order and the rules framed thereunder. It is an inherent duly of every person in a State governed by the rule of law to refrain from doing an act which is contrary to law and so it is also his duty to dissociate from, or purge himself of, any illegal action with which he may have unknowingly or inadvertently associated. This duty is all the more incumbent upon the Government, the executive organ of the State, which has the supreme duty of enforcing the rule of law. So if it is found that a property which was not an abandoned property but through some mistake or misconception was taken over as an abandoned property and that under the law in force it has not vested in the Government the Government has certainly on a discovery of such a mistake or misconception, the right, may the duty, to restore the property to the rightful owner forthwith, independently of any positive provision of law in this regard. So if it can be shown that the assets of the Respondent's firm were never abandoned properties and has never vested in the Government under any law, the impugned order of release may be taken as a valid and lawful order of release, although it was wrongly described to have been made under article 15(3) of the Order. 

 Now let us see if the assets of the Respondents firm were abandoned properties within the meaning of resident's Order No.16 of 1972 and as such vested in the Government of Bangladesh. 

 Under article 3 of the Order, the Management Board, Administrator, Autonomous or Semi-Autonomous body or the authority controlling or managing any industrial or commercial concern under this Order shall exercise powers and perform duties under the direct supervision and control of the Government of Bangladesh. 

 On the commencement of this Order, all those properties which have been defined as abandoned properties in article 2(1) of the Order vested in the Government of Bangladesh. 

 57. Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 was not repealed by this Order but it has been contended at the Bar that despite the absence of any repealing provision the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 was virtually abrogated by this new Order, which has laid down elaborate procedural provisions for the management of abandoned properties including those which may have been taken over under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972. This contention was advanced without noticing that the categories of the properties which can be taken over under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 are not the same as those which have vested in the Government and are controlled and managed as such under the provisions of President's Order No.16 of 1972 Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 relates to only industrial and commercial concerns and under the said Order the Government can take over the control and management, not only of the concern whose owners, directors and managers have left Bangladesh or are not available to control and manage the concern, which is in such a case, an abandoned property within the meaning of article 2(1) of President's Order No.16 of 1972, but also the concern whose owners, directors or managers, in the opinion of the Government, cannot be allowed in the public interest to control and manage the concern. The field of operation of the two Presidential Orders referred to above having not been the same, there seems to be no reason to take the view that there has been repeal of the earlier Presidential Order by necessary implication, even though there is no positive legislative provision in that respect. 

 Apart from the fact that it is a protected legislation under article 47(2) of the Constitution and has been specifically mentioned in the First Schedule to the Constitution there has been an amendment of this Order as late as on 15-12-72 by President's Order No.151 of 1972 which has been given retrospective effect from 3-1-1972. By the said amendment, clause 2(A) was added to article 2 of the Order, which has provided that the Government may from time to time publish for general information lists of industrial and commercial concerns taken over under the said Order. Had the Acting President's Order been repealed on 28-2-72 on the Promulgation of President's Order No.16 of 1972 the exercise of legislative power by way of amendment with regard to the said Acting President's Order could not have been possible. 

 58. Now let us see whether the assets of Respondent's firm in question had really vested in the Government as abandoned properties under President's Order No.16 of 1972. As it has already been noticed that if the said assets did vest in the Government under article 4 of President's Order No.16 of 1972, the order of release made by the Ministry of Industries on 24-1-76 could not have been made with lawful authority, but if it can be shown that the said assets did not at all vest in the Government and the Government's act of taking over the control and management of the same did not lead to any such legal consequence, there seems to be no impediment in the way of the Government in making the order releasing such assets. The case of the appellant Corporation as sought to be made out is that properties were taken over under Acting President's Order dated 30-12-71 and they had thereafter vested in the Government under the provisions of President's Order No.16 of 1972. 

 59. It appears that, by NOTIFICATION dated 7-3-72 purported to be made under what has been described as Acting President's Order dated 30-12-71, the management of M/S Masood Reza & Co., the firm of the Respondents, was taken over by the Ministry of Industries until further order. As we have seen, the Acting President's Order dated 30-12-71 was merely an amending Order, by which the Ministry of Industries and Natural Resources was given concurrent powers along with the Ministry of Commerce for the purposes of Acting President’s Order dated 26-12-71, which, of course, authorised such taking over. But on 3-1-72 the said Acting President Order dated 26-12-71, was repealed by article 6(1) of Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 and article 2(1) of the Order empowered the Government of Bangladesh to take over the control and management of certain Industrial and Commercial concerns. It may be contended that reference to Acting President's Order dated 3-12-71 in the NOTIFICATION dated 7-3-72 was clerical or accidental mistake. There is no doubt that such a reference was patently mistaken as on 7-3-72 there was no such Order in force as Acting President's Order dated 30-12-71 and ordinarily such taking over purported to be made under a non-existing law cannot be regarded to be lawful. It may, however, be argued that when on the date of such taking over the Government had the necessary jurisdiction, albeit under different legislation, to take over the control and management of such a concern and the Company was, as a matter of fact, taken over and managed by the Government for several years, the Court may hold that the action was taken under the right law, which may be read in the impugned NOTIFICATION in place of the mistaken reference. 

 61. We have already noticed that Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 has not been repealed and in spite of the promulgation of President’s Order No.16 of 1972 there are and certain areas where the said Presidential Order has no application but Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 may very well apply, namely, the case where, in the opinion of the Government of Bangladesh, the owners and the directors of any Industrial or Commercial concern cannot be allowed, in the public interest, to control or manage the concern. As regards the other contingencies contemplated under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972, namely, when the owners, directors and managers or majority of the owners, directors or managers have left Bangladesh or are not available to control or manage the concern have lost their significance so far as Acting President's Order No.1 of 1973 is concerned, after the promulgation of President's Order, No.16 of 1972 as they are covered by the provisions of the said Presidential Order, whereunder such concerns vested in the Government of Bangladesh on the promulgation of the said President' Order. The NOTIFICATION dated 7-3-72 cannot be read, in any view of the matter, as one under President's Order No.16 of 1972. Had it been so, there was no question of its management being taken over, as under article 4 of the Order all the properties would vest in the Government and they would be administered, controlled and managed and disposed of in accordance with the provisions of that Order. Having regard to the fact that Acting President's Order dated 26-12-71 was repealed by Acting President's Order No.1 of 172 and that it is provided therein that all the NOTIFICATIONs made under the repealed Order shall be deemed to have been made under the new Presidential Order, the NOTIFICATION dated 7-3-72 can at best be read as one under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972. If the NOTIFICATION be taken to be one under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 it must have been issued on the ground that the owners, director, or managers of the concern, in the opinion of the Government of Bangladesh, could not be allowed to control and manage the concern in the public interest. In such a case the properties were taken over for the control and management, but they did not vest in the Government and there seems to be no legal bar to the restoration of the concern to its owner i.e. if the Government is of opinion that in view of the changed circumstances, it is no longer necessary in the public interest to retain the control and management of the concern. 

 62. The answer to the second question also depends upon the fact whether on the placement of the Respondent’s firm under article 10(1) of President's Order No.27 of 1972, all the shares of the Respondents firm stood vested in the Government of Bangladesh under article 4 of the said Order. Under the said article, all the shares of the scheduled industrial enterprises or, as the case may be, the industrial enterprises placed under the Corporation by an order under clause (1) of article 10 shall stand vested in and allotted to the government. The respondent’s firm was not a scheduled industrial enterprises. The question, therefore, is whether it was lawfully placed under the Corporation under clause (1) of article 10 so that the legal consequences as contemplated in article 4 of the Order did follow. The Government may, by a NOTIFICATION under article 10(1) place an industrial enterprise, which had vested in the Government under President's Order No.16 of 1972 or was owned and managed by a Statutory Corporation. Obviously, the Respondent’s firm was not one of any of the two categories mentioned above, and as such it could not be lawfully placed under the Corporation under article 10(1) of the Order. 

 63. It has been contended, however by the learned Counsel for the Corporation, that in view of the clause (IA) of Article 10, which was added by President's Order No.153 of 1972, any Industrial enterprise if placed under a Corporation by an order notified in the Official Gazette under sub-clause (d) of clause (1) of article 10, whether it answers the description given therein or not, shall be deemed to have always been vested in the Government and no such order, as made under the said provision, shall be challenged on the ground that the industrial concern had not vested or was not liable to be vested in the Government. It appears that the contention of the learned Counsel could have been of much force, if the Respondent’s firm was an industrial enterprise. The provision of clause (1A) is attracted in case of an industrial enterprise which may be placed under a Corporation by an order under article 10(1) (d) of the Order. The Respondent’s firm being admittedly a commercial concern and not an industrial one, the provision of clause (1A) has no application in this case. Had it been an industrial enterprise, it would have been in my opinion, very difficult to avoid the operation of the said clause. Mr. Pal has contended that, even if it was a commercial concern, it is ancillary to, and has become an essential part of, the industrial enterprise managed by the Corporation and that in the circumstances of the case it may be deemed to be an industrial enterprise. There appears to be absolutely no reason to give an extended meaning to the term 'industrial enterprise' as used in President's Order No. 27 of 1972, which was promulgated, as the title, preamble and the enacting provisions of the Order indicate, for the nationalisation of certain industrial enterprises and for the establishment of Corporations for the control, supervision and co-ordination of such nationalised industrial enterprises. 

 "My Lords, I know of no such principle in our law nor was any authority for it cited. The illegality of an act is the same whether or not the actor has been misled by an assumption of authority on the part of Government officer however high or low in the hierarchy. I do not doubt that in criminal proceedings would be a material factor that the actor had been thus railed if knowledge was necessary element of the offence, and in any case it would have a bearing on the sentence to be imposed, but that is not the question. The question is whether the character of an act done in fact of a statutory prohibition is affected by the fact that it has been induced by a misleading assumption of authority. In my opinion, the answer is clearly: No." 

 66. The learned Judges of the High Court Division do not appear to have been correct in expressing the view that the observation of Lord Simonds, as quoted above, had relevance in a criminal case, and as such it did not diminish the persuasive value of the Robertson's case. What the noble Lord wanted to convey in the said observation is that in a criminal case a representation made by a department of the Crown contrary to law may affect in certain cases the question of mens rea of an offender and may also have some bearing on the question of sentence, but that cannot induce a Court of Law to accept an act as lawful, which is, in fact, unlawful. In the instant case their Lordships, however, have not applied, the principle of the Robertson's case on the view that the Corporation was not a Government department nor the Government itself, but have mainly based their decision on the view that the Corporation, as constituted under the President's Order No.27 of 1972 was bound by the NOTIFICATION issued by the Government. 

 67. Their Lordships seem to be of the view that inasmuch as the Government being the sovereign authority has made a pronouncement in the shape of a declaration by way of a NOTIFICATION and a citizen seeks to enforce it, a statutory Corporation constituted under President's Order No.27 of 1972 which operates, according to the provisions of the said Presidential Order, subject to the superintendence and control of the Government, cannot take the stand that it is not bound by the Govt. NOTIFICATION. Learned Counsel for Respondents Nos.1 to 3 has submitted, in support of the decision of the High Court Division, that the corporation being in the position of an agent vis-a-vis the Government and subject to its superintendence and control is not competent to challenge the validity of the Government NOTIFICATION and is bound to comply with it. 

 69. This proposition is, on the face of it, untenable. In a society governed by law, everybody is required to act accordingly to law and not to do a thing which is contrary to law. It is no doubt the duty of an agent to conduct the business of his principal according to the direction given by the principal, but it is no part of his duty to carry out a direction which is not according to law. If the principal gives an order to his agent which is not lawful, the compliance with such an order amounts to an unlawful act which, according to the basic law of the society, he is not bound to do. Even if there is a contract or engagement between them that whatever order or direction will be given by the principal stall be obeyed unquestioningly, such a contract or engagement shall not be enforceable in a Court of law, as it is void so far as the unlawful order is concerned, being contrary to law and against public policy. The general relationship between the principal and his agent, or master and servant, is regulated by the law of contract, which does not countenance such a proposition. So, if in a case of disobedience by an agent or servant of his principal's or master's order, the principal or master goes to a Court to enforce his order can it be said that the agent or servant, whose duty is to carry out the order of his principal or master, is estopped from pleading that the order is unlawful and, therefore, not enforceable. A Court of law may compel an agent or servant to do an act, which according to its judgment is lawful, if it is not otherwise barred, but a command of a principal or master cannot be deemed to be ipso facto lawful. It is a fundamental principal of judicial procedure in this country that a Court must be satisfied as to the enforceability of such a command after giving a proper opportunity to the person against whom the mandate of the Court has been sought, to substantiate his plea, if any. It is imperative for the Court to permit a person, against whom an order is sought, to show cause against such an order and in showing such cause the said person is certainly entitled to bring to the notice of the Court that the order which it is going to pass will be contrary to law. This is in conformity to the rule of natural justice which is naturally attracted in such a case. If, of course, there were a valid legislation disentitling an agent or servant to plead against an order sought to be made against him and compelling him to confess judgment in an action brought by his principal or master, the position might have been different. But we are not aware of any such legislation abrogating the rule of natural justice in such a case nor the decision of the learned Judges has been based upon any such law. Indeed, cases are not few where public servants, who are subject to the control of, and are bound, by the terms of their service, to carry out, the directions given by the Government, take recourse to the Courts of law for restraining the Government from enforcing certain orders against them, which, in their opinion, are unlawful, and Courts will not be within their powers to dismiss the servant's actions on the view that the set /ants are bound to obey the orders of their masters, right or wrong; but, on the other hand, they are required to decide the question of enforceability of the orders on their merits. 

 70. It has been argued that as the Corporation, which has been constituted for the purpose of control, supervision and coordination of certain industrial enterprises including these which may be placed under the Corporation by an order under article 10(1)(d) of President's Order No.27 of 1972 has no concern with the decision of the Government to place an industrial enterprise under it under the aforesaid provision and has no interest in such an enterprise except the duty of its control, supervision and co-ordination, if has no locus standi to question the decision of the Government to withdraw the said enterprise from its control and supervision, particularly in view of the fact that the Corporation is to act, according to the provision of the Presidential Order, subject to the superintendence and control of the Government. 

 71. The contention, that the Corporation being the agent of the Government and having had no concern with the questions of placement of an enterprise under it or its withdrawal is bound by the NOTIFICATIONs issued by the Government, leads us to the consideration of the nature of the functions of the Corporation and its position vis-a-vis the Government in relation to an industrial enterprise placed under it under Article 10(1) of the Order. In my opinion, its position is not that of an agent required merely to carry out the directions of the Government in respect of such an enterprise, but it’s position is that of a juristic person functioning in accordance with the provisions of law as contained in President's Order No.27 of 1972. The Government of the country which is the executive organ of the State undoubtedly exercises immense power for the administration of the affairs of the State. But the exercise of such powers must be subject to the law of the country. The Government is an abstract concept but its functions are carried on by a number of officers in various departments in accordance with the laws relating thereto. Now the provisions of President's Order No.27 of 1972 have laid down the procedures for nationalisation of certain industrial enterprises and for administration and management of such enterprises. Under the said Presidential Order, the Corporation as well as the Government have been allocated certain general and specific duties, which are to be performed in accordance with the provisions of the said Order. According to clause (1) of Article 11, the general direction and administration of the affairs and business of the Corporation shall vest in a Board of Directors which may exercise all powers and do all acts and things which maybe exercised or done by the Corporation and under clause (2) of the said article the Board shall be subject to the superintendence and control of the Government and shall be guided in the discharge of its function by such general or special instruction as may from time to time be given to it by the Government. Under article 13 the Chairman, and any other Director shall exercise such powers, perform such functions and discharge such duties as may be prescribed by rules or regulations made under the Order. Under article 17(1) the function of a Corporation is to control, supervise and co-ordinate, subject to any regulation made in this behalf, the activities, business and affairs of infer alia, the industrial enterprises placed under it by an order under clause (1) of article 10 and to establish and develop new industrial enterprises within their respective fields. Under clause (2) of the said article the Corporation shall have to exercise such powers as may be prescribed by rules or regulations made under the Order in respect of such industrial enterprises and under clause (3) thereof the Corporation shall in respect of such enterprises also exercise such of the powers of the Government as the Government may, by NOTIFICATION in the Official Gazette, delegate to the Corporation. Under article 22 the Corporation is to furnish to the Government such returns and statements as the Government may from time to time require. Under article 24 the Government may by NOTIFICATION in the Official Gazette make rules for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of the Order and under article 25 the Board of Directors may with, the previous approval of the Government make regulations to provide for all matters for which provision is necessary or expedient for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of this Order. 

 72. From the provisions referred to above it is clear that the Corporation is not, in the strict sense, an agent of the Government, but that all the actions of the Corporation in respect of an industrial enterprise placed, under article 10(1) (d) and also those of the Government in relation to such an enterprise are to be controlled and regulated by the provisions of the Order and the rules and regulations made under it. The Government may be the sovereign authority, in the sense that it is the supreme executive authority of the state, subject to whose control and superintendence, the Corporation discharges its functions in accordance with the provisions of the Order; nevertheless, it shall have to act according to law with respect to the enterprise which had been delivered to its care for the administration and management of the enterprise in accordance with the provisions of the Order, and, in my opinion, it will not be correct to say that it is a matter of no concern to a Corporation whether an enterprise which had been placed under it for administration and management is lawfully taken away from it or not, only because it did not participate in the Government's initial decision of placing the enterprise under it. The duty of the Corporation to administer and manage the enterprise in accordance with the provisions of the Order arises only after the placement of the enterprise under it and it having been deeply involved in the affairs of the enterprise since then, it will not be correct to say that what happens to the said enterprise is a matter of no concern to the Corporation. The Corporation has been invested with a legal personality, as it appears from article 10(2) of the Order, which provides, inter alia, that the Corporation shall be a body corporate, having a perpetual succession and shall by its name sue and be sued, and there can therefore be no doubt that such a Corporation has the necessary legal competence to raise a question as to the legality of an act which seeks to affect its scheme of administration and management of the enterprise which was purported to have been lawfully entrusted to it for such administration and management. When such a question is raised, the Court is bound to give its decision on the question in the light of the law applicable thereto. The Corporation also has its duties and responsibilities under the said Presidential Order and is accountable for all of its actions. If in course of discharging its duties which are regulated by laws the Corporation comes across an order of the Government which, in its opinion, is not in accordance with the provisions of the Older nor any other law, it will be its duty not to implement such an order but to place the matter before the appropriate authority for proper decision in the matter. 

 73. There is, however, another aspect of the case. When the jurisdiction of the Court of law has been invoked under Article 102(1) of the Constitution to make an order directing the Corporation to restore the Respondents firm to Respondents No.1 to 3 in compliance with the Government order of release of the enterprise on cancellation of its placement under the Corporation and the Court has called upon the Corporation to show cause why such an order should not be made in such a case, the Corporation has the bounden duty apart from the question of its powers and duties under the said Presidential Order, to state before the Court why it has not complied with the Government order and the Court is bound to decide upon the legality and enforceability of the Government order after giving a hearing to the Respondent Corporation. 

 74. The duty of the Court has been very clearly spelt out in the provisions of Article 102 of the Constitution under which the judgment under appeal was pronounced. Under the said provision, the High Court Division can make an order requiring the Corporation to act in accordance with the Government order of release and cancellation of placement of the Respondent’s firm, only when the Court judicially decides that the said orders are lawful and the Corporation 'is required by law' to act in accordance with the said orders. It will not suffice to say that it is a Government order and the appellant Corporation, which operates under President's Order No.27 of 1972 is subject to the control and superintendence of the Government and is therefore bound to carry it out, because the High Court Division is enjoined by the law as incorporated in Article 102 of the Constitution, to come to a decision that the Corporation 'is required by law" to restore the disputed firm to the Respondents. If the Corporation acts frivolously in raising untenable objections to the Government orders, it is for the Government to whose control and superintendence it is subject, to take appropriate action consistent with the rules of business applicable to the case. It relates to the internal management of the Corporation and the Court has nothing to do with it. 

 75. On all these considerations I do not think that there is any legal bar preventing the Corporation from raising, in an appropriate Court of law, a question as to the legality of an order affecting its administration and management of an enterprise placed under it under Article 10(1) of the Order, even though the said order is purported to have been made on behalf of the Government which exercise a kind of control and superintendence in accordance with the provisions of the said order. 

 76. But as I have already held that the assets of the Respondent's firm did not vest in the Government and that as such the order of release made by Government cannot be said to be to be unlawful. I concur with the opinion of any learned brother Mr. Justice Munim that these appeals should be dismissed.
